title: Black Parents Should Not Have to Choose Between Tutoring and Therapy
author: Augustus Mays
summary: Augustus Mays of EdTrust reads Nikole Hannah-Jones's essay first as a Black father, naming the dilemma many Black families face: choose an academically stronger school and later need therapy for isolation and racism, or choose a culturally affirming school and later need tutoring to make up for weak instruction. He acknowledges that many families cannot afford either remedy and have only their neighborhood school. Mays rejects the narrative that Black children or families are the problem, and cites New York's move to sunset the Regents exam as a possible sign of low expectations. He argues that no single family can repair unfair funding, workforce instability, or generations of disinvestment, and he opposes shifting public dollars to private schools. His answer is an excellent neighborhood public school guaranteed to every family, which EdTrust's forthcoming A Nation of Promise agenda aims to advance.
points: Mays frames the Black parent's dilemma as a forced choice between tutoring and therapy.
He notes that therapy, tutoring, private tuition, and moving are all beyond the reach of many families.
New York's graduation rate reached 85 percent while only 56 percent passed the Algebra I Regents, a gap he reads as a warning about low expectations.
Individual families, he argues, cannot fix funding formulas, educator workforce problems, or disinvestment by themselves.
He calls for choice to begin with an excellent neighborhood public school rather than vouchers for private institutions.
quotes: When I read Nikole Hannah-Jones’ deeply personal essay, “ In Fighting for Every Black Child, Did I Betray My Own?,” I did not read it first as an education advocate. I read it as a Black father.

Choose the school with greater academic opportunities, and you may later need therapy to help your child process the racism, isolation, lowered expectations, and daily indignities of being one of only a few Black students in the building.
For millions of parents, there is one choice – the neighborhood school – and they do everything they can within that constraint to make sure it sees their child’s promise.
Is the Regents exam imperfect? Absolutely. But I worry this choice may be influenced by the bias of low expectations.
No individual family, regardless of its income, connections, or commitment, can compensate for a system stacked against them.
Parents deserve choices, and that choice must start at an excellent neighborhood public school. Not as something you move, buy, or maneuver into, but as something that is guaranteed.
